newsitem.title: UK: Larger trade gap offers perilous cure for UK boom.
newsitem.headline: Larger trade gap offers perilous cure for UK boom.

text.p: Balance of payments problems are usually the stuff of politicians' nightmares, but Britain's new Labour government may actually be pinning its hopes on a worsening in the trade position.

Analysts say a wider balance of payments deficit could help to slow strong and potentially inflationary economic growth, and quash the pound's exuberance, which has inflicted serious pain on exporters.

"Seldom have Treasury forecasts been so dependent on a deterioration in net trade in goods and the pound," Yamaichi chief economist John Shepperd said. "The government must be sitting around saying "good grief, we hope the current account gets worse and the pound falls."

Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown predicted on Wednesday that Britain would post a current account deficit of 6.0 billion pounds ($10.1 billion) in 1997, increasing to 9.0 billion in 1998. By contrast, the deficit in 1996 was just 500 million pounds.
Britain is still a long way from the balance of payments' crises which dogged it during the 1980s boom.

But relying on a fall in exports to pull the economy back down to a steady "trend" growth of 2.5 percent next year from the official forecast of 3.25 for this year is nevertheless fraught with danger.

"What we're likely to get is the opposite of what the economy actually needs," CIBC chief economist David Coleman said. "We're going to get another squeeze on exporters when what we actually need is less consumer demand."

So far British exports have held up remarkably well in the face of an overall surge in the pound of 20 percent -- 30 percent against the deutschemark alone -- but analysts say the export picture will change next year.

"The impact of the depreciation in the Japanese yen against the U.S. dollar took around 18 months to filter through to trade and we're probably looking at a similar timescale for sterling," Coleman said.
Sterling began to rocket in August last year.

Wednesday's budget gave it another fillip by fuelling speculation that interest rates would have to rise to curb domestic demand as the bulk of tax increases were aimed at the corporate rather than the buoyant consumer sector.
At the moment, markets pay no attention to British trade data both because they have conspicuously failed to show a clear trend and because they are simply not fashionable as an economic indicator.
But sentiment towards economic indicators is notoriously fickle -- yesterday's "wallflower" is often tomorrow's belle of the ball.
"No-one really wants to know about trade at the moment but I think it's set to become much more of an issue," HSBC UK economist Jonathan Loynes said.
Soaring trade deficits tend eventually to lead to losses of confidence in currencies and Britain has a particularly sad history in this respect.

Worries over a deterioration in the balance of payments in 1976 led to a sterling crisis under the last Labour government, ousted in 1979. Some commentators believe the sterling crisis was ultimately responsible for the party's subsequent 18 years in opposition, which only ended in May this year.
At present the prospect of higher interest rates is continuing to lure investors into the pound.

Many economists expect the Bank of England, newly empowered by Brown to determine monetary policy, to increase Britain's 6.5 percent interest rates by up to 1/2 percentage point next week to check inflationary pressures.

But once the perception is that interest rates have peaked, the pound is likely to come under pressure. Britain's productivity has improved, but not by enough to weather such a sharp appreciation in the pound, analysts say.
"The chances of a sterling crisis further down the line have certainly increased after the budget," HSBC's Loynes said.

While Brown said that his budget would help to address the imbalance in the economy between the sluggish export sector on one side and the robust service and consumer sector on the other, analysts believe he may have actually worsened the situation.

A steady deterioration in the trade position will gradually throw up worries over other economic measures such as inflation and the strength of consumer demand, especially as millions of Britons will receive 30 billion pounds' worth of free shares as mutually owned building societies turn themselves into banks.
"The government is almost relying on the trade deficit to deteriorate as a pressure valve, but this doesn't seem to be the safest way of cooling the economy," Loynes said.
